content: Studies have indicated that a diet enriched with omega-3 essential fatty acids may exert anti-inflammatory effects, which could be beneficial for chronic conditions such as cystic fibrosis. This review aimed to evaluate whether omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation reduces morbidity and mortality in individuals with cystic fibrosis and to identify any associated adverse events. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing omega-3 fatty acid supplements to placebo in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Five studies involving 106 participants (both children and adults) were included. The duration of the studies and the interventions varied. Two studies compared omega-3 fatty acids to olive oil over six weeks, one study compared omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids to control capsules over three months, one study compared a liquid dietary supplement containing omega-3 fatty acids to one without over six months, and one study compared omega-3 fatty acids to placebo over 12 months. The risk of bias was assessed for each study. Three studies had a low risk of bias for randomization, while the risk was unclear in the other two studies. All studies had an unclear risk of bias for allocation concealment. Three studies adequately blinded participants, but one study had a high risk of bias for selective reporting, and four studies had an unclear risk. Two studies reported on respiratory exacerbations. One study with 43 participants found no change in antibiotic usage at three months. Another study with 15 participants reported a reduction in pulmonary exacerbations and cumulative antibiotic days in the supplement group over 12 months compared to the previous year, but no data were available for the control group. However, the evidence quality was very low, making it uncertain whether supplementation had any effect on these outcomes. Regarding adverse events, one six-week study with 12 participants reported no difference in diarrhea between the omega-3 and placebo groups. However, the evidence quality was very low, leaving uncertainty about the effect of supplementation on this outcome. Another study reported an increase in steatorrhea, requiring participants to increase their daily dose of pancreatic enzymes. Three studies had already adjusted pancreatic enzyme doses at the start of the study to reduce the incidence of steatorrhea. One study with 43 participants reported stomach pains at three months, but it was unclear whether this occurred in the treatment or control group. A six-week study with 19 participants reported three asthma exacerbations, leading to the exclusion of participants, as corticosteroid treatment could influence fatty acid metabolism. Four studies reported on lung function. One six-week study with 19 participants observed an increase in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC), but the evidence quality was very low, making it uncertain whether supplementation had any effect on lung function. The remaining studies reported no differences in lung function at three months, six months, or one year. No deaths were reported in any of the five studies. Four studies assessed clinical variables. One study reported an increase in Schwachman score and weight, along with a reduction in sputum volume, in the supplementation group compared to placebo at three months. However, the data were not analyzable. Three other studies reported no differences in weight at six weeks, body mass index (BMI) standard deviation score at six months, or BMI Z score at 12 months. The evidence quality for these outcomes was very low. Three studies measured biochemical markers of fatty acid status. One study found an increase in eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) content in serum phospholipids in the omega-3 group compared to placebo at three months, along with a significant decrease in the n-6/n-3 ratio. However, the evidence quality was very low, making it uncertain whether these changes were due to supplementation. A six-month crossover study reported higher EPA content in neutrophil membranes in the supplement group compared to placebo, but no difference in DHA membrane concentration. Additionally, the leukotriene B4 to leukotriene B5 ratio was lower in the omega-3 group at six months. A one-year study reported a greater increase in the essential fatty acid profile and a decrease in arachidonic acid (AA) levels in the treatment group compared to placebo. The authors concluded that regular omega-3 supplementation may offer limited benefits for individuals with cystic fibrosis, with relatively few adverse effects. However, the quality of evidence across all outcomes was very low, making it insufficient to draw firm conclusions or recommend routine use of omega-3 supplements in this population. A large, long-term, multicenter, randomized controlled trial is needed to determine any significant therapeutic effects and to assess the influence of disease severity, dosage, and treatment duration. Future research should also consider the need for additional pancreatic enzymes when providing omega-3 supplementation or olive oil placebo capsules. Further studies are required to determine the precise dose of pancreatic enzymes needed.
